Reproducing DeWeese and Zador (2004) from CRCNS data set ac-2¶

Paper. DeWeese MR, Zador AM (2004). Shared and private variability in the auditory cortex. J Neurophysiol 92:1840-1855. doi:10.1152/jn.00197.2004. The claims file (claims/crcns-ac-2/10.1152-jn.00197.2004.yaml) was written from the version of record (text extracted from the journal PDF, with its Methods and figure legends; the paper has no supplement and links no code).

Data set. CRCNS ac-2, doi:10.6080/K0G44N6R, read from the public bucket crcnsarchive (ac-2/crcns-ac-2.tar.gz and ac-2/crcns-ac-2-docs_and_scripts.tar.gz). CRCNS data sets are not versioned, so the version is recorded as unversioned; the only published content is this one, and the paper cites none. It is pinned by the MD5 sums of the data set's checksums.md5: crcns-ac-2.tar.gz af006ca3530e7f615a37d0548ba86cf2 and crcns-ac-2-docs_and_scripts.tar.gz 6ffd46575e78b3f8a2ad3efb9f95008a. The notebook computes both sums from the bytes it streams and compares them (below), so a later change of the files is detected. The data tar is a gzipped tar, which cannot be read by range; it is streamed once into memory (about 30 s) and nothing is written to disk.

What the data set holds. The 33 anesthetized whole-cell recordings of the variability analysis, 29 of them with a simultaneous LFP; six recordings after TTX (the paper's mEPSPs); one awake recording that belongs to a later paper and is not used.

import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

import ac2

pd.set_option("display.width", 220)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

started = time.time()
D = ac2.load()
N = D["neurons"]
print(f"data set {ac2.DATASET} ({ac2.DATASET_VERSION}, doi:{ac2.DATASET_DOI}) loaded in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")
print("MD5 of the streamed files:", D["md5"])
print("MD5 in checksums.md5:     ", ac2.MD5)
print("Same:", D["md5"] == ac2.MD5)

The data set's files agree with its documentation on the counts: 33 anesthetized neurons, 13 under pentobarbital, 3 with diazepam and 17 under urethane (the paper's group sizes), and 29 with the flag was_LFP_recorded (the paper's 29 with a stable LFP). Each trace is 600 samples (150 ms at the documented 4 kHz) and starts at its nominal place in the sweeps (200 ms + 500 ms per tone, minus 15 ms): every trace equals its piece of the sweep minus its stored baseline, to floating point, and no shift is needed. The documentation says the stimulus-locked traces were corrected for a mismatch of the tone onset times; the traces are not shifted against the stored sweeps, so either the sweeps carry the same correction or none was applied; this cannot be told from the files. Every trace is relative to the mean of its first 15 ms, as documented. Each neuron's cell_specific_parameters.m gives a stable epoch (first_cycle to last_cycle, cycles of 32 tones) and a spike threshold; the files do not describe them for these neurons (the TTX neurons' copies of the file describe both fields).

Repetitions per tone are taken as the length of each neuron's stable epoch. They match the paper: mean 18, range 10 to 63 (printed above). No two neurons share their traces. The neuron names carry 21 recording days, the paper's 21 animals; names with the same day are listed as the same animal in the docs table ("same").

In [4]:
# The clock of the traces against the tone sequence: the tone explains the response after onset
# (peak in the 50 ms after onset), and not the 100 ms before onset, taken from the sweeps. The
# null is the same measure with the tone labels permuted at random over the trials.
def eta2(h, labels):
    df = pd.DataFrame({"h": h, "g": labels})
    ss_b = (df.groupby("g").h.transform("mean") - df.h.mean()) ** 2
    return ss_b.sum() / ((df.h - df.h.mean()) ** 2).sum()

rng_clock = np.random.default_rng(1)
clock = []
for name, n in N.items():
    idx = np.flatnonzero(ac2.stable(n) & ~ac2.spikes(n, "cell"))
    labels = n["tone"][idx]
    post = n["r"][idx, ac2.PRE:ac2.PRE + 200].max(1)
    pre = n["pre_wc"][idx].max(1) - n["pre_wc"][idx].mean(1)
    null = [eta2(post, rng_clock.permutation(labels)) for _ in range(20)]
    row = {"neuron": name, "post_onset": eta2(post, labels), "pre_onset": eta2(pre, labels),
           "null_median": np.median(null), "null_max": np.max(null)}
    if ac2.has_lfp(n):
        lpost = np.abs(n["lfp"][idx, ac2.PRE:ac2.PRE + 200]).max(1)
        lpre = np.abs(n["pre_lfp"][idx] - n["pre_lfp"][idx].mean(1, keepdims=True)).max(1)
        row.update(lfp_post=eta2(lpost, labels), lfp_pre=eta2(lpre, labels),
                   lfp_null_max=max(eta2(lpost, rng_clock.permutation(labels)) for _ in range(20)))
    row["evoked_mV"] = float(n["r"][idx, ac2.PRE + 40:ac2.PRE + 200].mean())
    # Response onset: first time after onset where the mean over all tones exceeds 1 mV, and the
    # largest |mean| in the 15 ms before onset and the first 5 ms after it.
    grand = n["r"][idx].mean(0)
    above = np.flatnonzero(grand[ac2.PRE:] > 1.0)
    row["onset_latency_ms"] = above[0] / ac2.FS * 1000 if len(above) else np.nan
    row["max_abs_mean_-15_to_5ms"] = float(np.abs(grand[:ac2.PRE + 20]).max())
    clock.append(row)
clock = pd.DataFrame(clock).set_index("neuron")
print("Fraction of variance explained by the tone (eta squared), after and before onset, with the null:")
print(clock.round(3).to_string())
print("\nWhole cell: post-onset eta2 above the largest of 20 permuted values in",
      int((clock.post_onset > clock.null_max).sum()), "of", len(clock), "neurons; pre-onset above it in",
      int((clock.pre_onset > clock.null_max).sum()))
lc = clock.dropna(subset=["lfp_post"])
print("LFP: post-onset above the largest permuted value in", int((lc.lfp_post > lc.lfp_null_max).sum()), "of", len(lc),
      "; pre-onset above it in", int((lc.lfp_pre > lc.lfp_null_max).sum()))

Whole cell: post-onset eta2 above the largest of 20 permuted values in 33 of 33 neurons; pre-onset above it in 26
LFP: post-onset above the largest permuted value in 27 of 29 ; pre-onset above it in 11

The tone sequence of the documentation is aligned with the traces: in every neuron the tone explains the response after onset beyond the largest of 20 permuted labellings, and the mean response rises above 1 mV only after onset (onset_latency_ms, printed above), with the mean trace flat from 15 ms before to 5 ms after onset. The 100 ms before onset is also tone-dependent beyond the null in most neurons; this is expected with a fixed tone order, since each tone is always preceded by the same tone 500 ms earlier, whose slow after-effects fall in that window. So this contrast cannot separate an offset from a response, and the alignment rests on the onset latency and the post-onset tuning. The LFP and the whole-cell traces are cut from the same sweeps at the same samples (the sweeps file holds both channels), so they share the clock.

# Units and ranges of the variables used.
allr = np.concatenate([n["r"][ac2.stable(n)].ravel()[::50] for n in N.values()])
alll = np.concatenate([n["lfp"][ac2.stable(n)].ravel()[::50] for n in N.values() if ac2.has_lfp(n)])
print("r (mV, relative to the 15-ms baseline), 0.1 / 50 / 99.9 percentiles:", np.percentile(allr, [0.1, 50, 99.9]).round(2))
print("lfp (mV after the gain correction), 0.1 / 50 / 99.9 percentiles:", np.percentile(alll, [0.1, 50, 99.9]).round(3))
base = pd.Series({name: np.median(n["rbaseline"][ac2.stable(n)]) for name, n in N.items()})
print("Median recorded baseline per neuron (mV, uncorrected): %.1f to %.1f" % (base.min(), base.max()))
gains = info.loc[list(N), ["axogaincorrection_wholecell", "axogaincorrection_LFP"]]

      "; LFP gain corrections:", pd.Series(gains.axogaincorrection_LFP.astype(float)).value_counts(dropna=False).to_dict())
lfp_param = {name: n["params"].get("Axo_gain_correction_of_lfp") for name, n in N.items()}

The paper's procedure, under every reading¶

All claims on variability use the same per-tone values: PSP heights, q, and q after each stage of Figure 6 (PSP-based culling, LFP-based culling, estimation with its overfitting correction, and both cullings with estimation). They are computed here once per reading of the open details (claims file header, details 1 to 7), and each claim's section reads them. The main reading:

  • trials: the stable epoch of each neuron (first_cycle to last_cycle), without spike trials;
  • spikes: the data set's per-neuron spikethresh above the trace's baseline (an assumption; see below), with the claims file's rule, a fast rise to above -20 mV after the 12 mV junction potential correction, as a reading (6);
  • peak of the mean PSP searched over the whole trace after onset (detail 1a), the culling window as a reading (1b);
  • peak-to-trough height over the culling window (2a), the whole trace as a reading (2b);
  • variance over N - 1 (3), N as a reading;
  • negative scale factors removed in PSP-based culling too (4a), not removed as a reading (4b);
  • the 3 mV and 15 mV criteria on the mean before culling (5a), after it as a reading (5b);
  • overfitting correction with the mean over 20 shuffles (7); per neuron and per tone give the same tone average, so one is run.

PSP-based culling comes first and LFP-based culling is then run on the trials it keeps, its mean LFP recomputed over them, as the Figure 6 legend has it ("we repeat the above procedure after first performing the PSP-based culling procedure"); deciding each culling on the full ensemble and keeping the trials neither removes is a reading ("cullings intersected"). Heights are measured once on the full ensemble (a choice stated in ac2.py); the Methods say only that q is "recalculated" after culling, so heights taken again against the peak of the mean of the trials each culling keeps are a reading ("heights re-measured after culling").

In [6]:

Spike trials. The claims file's header treats spike detection as a standard choice, "a fast rise to above -20 mV", that "can change only the few trials with spikes" (detail 6). That rule is run here as written: the trace, corrected by the paper's 12 mV junction potential, exceeds -20 mV, and its largest rise between samples exceeds 10 mV/ms (a standard choice for the "fast rise"). The data set gives each neuron its own threshold (spikethresh in cell_specific_parameters.m, 28 to 55 mV above the trace's baseline), which the TTX neurons' copies of the same file describe as the "height of threshold (mV) above BASELINE/REST for spike detection/removal". The table below gives, per neuron, the trials each rule removes and their largest rise, and the figure shows trials that only one rule removes.

In [7]:
# Trials each spike rule removes, per neuron (stable epoch), with the largest rise between samples.
rows = []
for name, n in N.items():
    st = ac2.stable(n)
    rise = ac2.max_rise(n["r"])
    recorded = (n["r"] + n["rbaseline"][:, None]).max(1)
    masks = {"above -20 mV uncorrected": (recorded > -20) & st,
             "above -20 mV corrected": (recorded - ac2.JUNCTION_MV > -20) & st,
             "fast rise and above -20 mV corrected (claims file)": ac2.spikes(n, "claims") & st,
             "spikethresh (data set)": ac2.spikes(n, "cell") & st}
    row = {"neuron": name, "spikethresh": n["params"]["spikethresh"]}
    for label, m in masks.items():
        row[label] = int(m.sum())
        row[label + ", max rise mV/ms"] = f"{rise[m].min():.1f} to {rise[m].max():.1f}" if m.any() else ""
    row["spikethresh only"] = int((masks["spikethresh (data set)"] & ~masks["fast rise and above -20 mV corrected (claims file)"]).sum())
    row["claims file only"] = int((~masks["spikethresh (data set)"] & masks["fast rise and above -20 mV corrected (claims file)"]).sum())
    row["max rise, 99th percentile of all trials"] = float(np.percentile(rise[st], 99))
    rows.append(row)
spk = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("neuron")
print(spk.round(1).to_string())
print("\nTotals:", spk.select_dtypes("number").drop(columns=["spikethresh", "max rise, 99th percentile of all trials"]).sum().to_dict())

# The trials only spikethresh removes, by kind: the corrected potential crosses -20 mV with a rise
# below the 10 mV/ms of the claims file's rule; it stays below -20 mV with a fast rise (above 5
# mV/ms); it stays below -20 mV with a slow rise (at most 5 mV/ms).
kinds = []
for name, n in N.items():
    st = ac2.stable(n)
    only = ac2.spikes(n, "cell") & ~ac2.spikes(n, "claims") & st
    if not only.any():
        continue
    peak = (n["r"] + n["rbaseline"][:, None] - ac2.JUNCTION_MV).max(1)[only]
    rise = ac2.max_rise(n["r"])[only]
    kinds.append({"neuron": name, "spikethresh only": int(only.sum()),
                  "above -20 mV, rise < 10": int((peak > -20).sum()),
                  "below -20 mV, rise > 5": int(((peak <= -20) & (rise > ac2.SLOW_DVDT)).sum()),
                  "below -20 mV, rise <= 5": int(((peak <= -20) & (rise <= ac2.SLOW_DVDT)).sum()),
                  "peak mV (corrected)": f"{peak.min():.1f} to {peak.max():.1f}"})
kinds = pd.DataFrame(kinds).set_index("neuron")

Of 342 trials that spikethresh removes over the 33 neurons, the claims file's rule (fast rise and above -20 mV after correction) also removes 155. It removes 162 in all, 7 that spikethresh keeps (table above). The 187 trials that only spikethresh removes are of three kinds (second table). 114 cross -20 mV after correction with a largest rise below the 10 mV/ms chosen here for the "fast rise": broad spikes that peak between -20 and +7 mV, as in 102500md02 (25 trials), 102900md04 (26) and 102900md02 (11), and the slow depolarizations of 102800md02 (24) and 100300md02 (14). In 102800md02 these rise by 1.5 to 2.9 mV/ms, no faster than that neuron's 99th percentile over all trials (2.9 mV/ms), and go from about -70 to -10 mV over about 50 ms; they may be regenerative events that QX-314 leaves in place of fast spikes, or large PSPs, which the data cannot tell apart. 44 stay below -20 mV with a rise above 5 mV/ms, narrow spikes as in 022301md01 (22 trials) and 100500md01 (10). 29 stay below -20 mV with a rise of at most 5 mV/ms.

The spike rule changes the results (overview above). Two further rules bound the choice: the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise (311 trials) gives 4.43 mV, close to spikethresh's 4.58, and spikethresh with the slow events kept (largest rise above 5 mV/ms, 247 trials) gives 5.11 mV, about two thirds of the way to the claims file's rule with the 10 mV/ms rise (5.35 mV, 162 trials). So the difference between the claims file's rule and spikethresh comes from the 10 mV/ms rise criterion, and most of it from the slow events. Applied without the correction and without the fast rise, as in the earlier version of this notebook, -20 mV marks 513 trials, many of them subthreshold PSPs (in 102400md01, 73 trials with largest rises from 0.5 mV/ms). Under step 1.6 of the protocol all four rules are shown for every claim. The per-neuron threshold, the authors' own parameter, is adopted as an assumption, and outcomes that differ between the rules are marked as resting on it. If the slow events are large PSPs, removing them selects on the response and lowers q.

fig3a-reliable-neuron¶

For the most reliable neuron, the responses to 20 presentations of a 32-kHz tone cluster tightly about the mean (q = 0.23 mV), and its variability averaged over the 26 tones with a mean PSP above 3 mV is 0.88 mV.

This section comes first because fig2-stereotyped-shape uses the neuron it identifies.

In [8]:
def tone_table(label, name):
    return pd.DataFrame([{k: v for k, v in r.items() if np.isscalar(v)} for r in PT[label][name]]).set_index("tone")

for label in ("main", SPK, SPK_ANY, SPK_SLOW, "peak in culling window (1b)", "variance over N (3)"):
    df = S[label]
    best = df.q.idxmin()
    near = (df.q - 0.88).abs().idxmin()
    tt = tone_table(label, best)

          f" neuron nearest 0.88 mV: {near} ({df.q[near]:.3f}); repetitions {int(cells.reps[best])};"

Result: reproduced. The neuron with the lowest tones, 022801md01b, has tones = 0.88 mV over 26 tones with a mean PSP above 3 mV and 20 repetitions per tone, as in the paper, under the main reading and with the claims file's spike rule (no spike trials in this neuron). Its q for the 31,118-Hz tone is 0.229 mV (reading a of "32 kHz", the nearest tone); for 34,448 Hz (reading b) it is 0.648 mV. The neuron and the 0.88 mV do not depend on the spike rule or the peak window; with the variance over N, tones is 0.832 mV and q at 31,118 Hz 0.217 mV, both within tolerance. The two further spike rules give the same values. The panels match Figure 3A, which is labelled 022801md01b: the 20 responses to 31 kHz rise about 15 ms after onset to about 15 mV and decay over about 60 ms, two of them falling below baseline late in the trace, and the q of the 26 tones spread from 0.23 to 2.04 mV around their mean of 0.88, as in the inset (0 to 2 mV).

fig2-stereotyped-shape¶

Tones evoke brief, short-latency PSPs in all neurons. In the example neuron the mean responses to the 32 tones peak 27 to 42 ms after onset with heights of 1.2 to 18 mV, and are similar in shape once normalized and aligned.

def mean_traces(n):
    idx_ok = ac2.stable(n) & ~ac2.spikes(n, "cell")
    return {int(t): n["r"][idx_ok & (n["tone"] == t)].astype(float).mean(0) for t in ac2.TONE_ORDER}

for window, (lo, hi) in {"after onset (1a)": (ac2.PRE, ac2.TRACE), "culling window (1b)": (ac2.PRE, 400)}.items():
    mt = mean_traces(N[EXAMPLE])
    lat = {t: (lo + np.argmax(m[lo:hi]) - ac2.PRE) / ac2.FS * 1000 for t, m in mt.items()}
    hgt = {t: m[lo:hi].max() for t, m in mt.items()}
    print(f"[{window}] {EXAMPLE}: latency to peak {min(lat.values()):.2f} to {max(lat.values()):.2f} ms;"
          f" peak height {min(hgt.values()):.2f} to {max(hgt.values()):.2f} mV (32 tones)")
lat = pd.Series({t: (ac2.PRE + np.argmax(m[ac2.PRE:]) - ac2.PRE) / ac2.FS * 1000 for t, m in mt.items()})
hgt = pd.Series({t: m[ac2.PRE:].max() for t, m in mt.items()})
print("Latencies (ms) by tone:", lat.round(2).sort_index().to_dict())
print("Tones with latency outside 24.3-46.2 ms:", lat[(lat < 24.3) | (lat > 46.2)].round(2).to_dict())

# Shape: normalize each mean trace to its peak and align it on the peak; window = the culling
# window placed for a tone at the median latency.
med = ac2.PRE + int(round(np.median(lat.values) * ac2.FS / 1000))
before, after = med, 400 - med
aligned = []
for t, m in mt.items():
    pk = ac2.PRE + int(np.argmax(m[ac2.PRE:]))
    padded = np.pad(m, (before, after), mode="edge")       # edge values where the window runs off the trace
    aligned.append(padded[pk:pk + before + after] / m[pk])
aligned = np.array(aligned)
avg = aligned.mean(0)
cors = np.array([np.corrcoef(x, avg)[0, 1] for x in aligned])
print(f"Aligned traces: {len(aligned)} of 32, window {-before / 4:.2f} to {after / 4:.2f} ms around the peak; correlation with their average: median {np.median(cors):.3f},"
      f" min {cors.min():.3f}, 10th percentile {np.percentile(cors, 10):.3f}")
# Unaligned (no shift), for reference.
raw = np.array([m[:400] / m[ac2.PRE:].max() for m in mt.values()])
cr = np.array([np.corrcoef(x, raw.mean(0))[0, 1] for x in raw])
print(f"Without alignment: median correlation {np.median(cr):.3f}")

# All neurons: latency of the mean response to each neuron's largest tone, with the peak (and the
# largest tone) searched after onset (1a) or in the culling window, up to 85 ms after onset (1b),
# and the response onset of the data check (mean over all tones first above 1 mV).
big = []
for name, n in N.items():
    m = mean_traces(n)
    row = {"neuron": name}
    for label, hi in (("1a", ac2.TRACE), ("1b", 400)):
        t_big = max(m, key=lambda t: m[t][ac2.PRE:hi].max())
        row[f"tone ({label})"] = t_big
        row[f"peak mV ({label})"] = m[t_big][ac2.PRE:hi].max()
        row[f"latency ms ({label})"] = np.argmax(m[t_big][ac2.PRE:hi]) / ac2.FS * 1000
    row["response onset ms"] = clock.onset_latency_ms[name]
    big.append(row)
big = pd.DataFrame(big).set_index("neuron")
for label in ("1a", "1b"):
    x = big[f"latency ms ({label})"]
    print(f"\nLargest tone per neuron ({label}): latency {x.min():.2f} to {x.max():.2f} ms (median {x.median():.2f});"
          f" within 50 ms in {int((x <= 50).sum())} of {len(x)}")
o = big["response onset ms"]
print(f"Response onset: {o.min():.2f} to {o.max():.2f} ms (median {o.median():.2f}); within 50 ms in {int((o <= 50).sum())} of {len(o)}")
print(big[big["latency ms (1a)"] > 50].round(2).to_string())

Result: partially reproduced. In 022801md01b (20 trials per tone, the Figure 2 legend's 20 presentations) the mean responses to the 32 tones peak 26.5 to 41.5 ms after onset with heights of 1.19 to 18.12 mV, within the widened ranges (24.3 to 46.2 ms; 1.08 to 19.8 mV), under both peak windows. Normalized and aligned on their peaks, the 32 mean traces correlate with their average with a median r of 0.991 (minimum 0.933), above the 0.9 the criterion sets. The "all neurons" part does not hold under the claims file's 50-ms bound: the mean response to each neuron's largest tone peaks within 50 ms of onset in 19 of 33 neurons, with the peak searched after onset (20.75 to 115.5 ms, median 45.25) or in the culling window (20.75 to 84.75 ms). The responses begin early in every neuron: the mean over all tones first exceeds 1 mV 14.25 to 38.5 ms after onset in 32 neurons (021401md02 never exceeds it). The late peaks of the other 14 come from responses that keep rising after onset, which the 50-ms bound on the peak counts against. The panels match Figure 2 (labelled 022801md01b, the neuron identified in fig3a): mean responses of 1 to 18 mV that rise about 15 ms after onset, and normalized, aligned traces that overlap closely, with a few decaying below zero.

fig3b-total-variability-distribution¶

Across the 33 neurons the tone-averaged variability index ranges over more than an order of magnitude, from below 1 to above 10 mV; about a fifth (7/33) have low variability (1 to 2 mV) and about half (18/33) have high variability (4 to 12 mV).

Result: reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption and on detail 1). Under the main reading tones ranges from 0.88 to 11.21 mV (below 1 and above 10 mV). 18 neurons lie between 4 and 12 mV. 6 lie strictly between 1 and 2 mV, outside 7 +- 0.7. Under the criterion's second reading of the low count (q < 2 mV, which includes the 0.88 mV example neuron) it is 7. Both counts hold under that reading. With the claims file's spike rule the counts are 5 (6 below 2 mV) and 20, both outside, which would give not reproduced. With the peak in the culling window (1b) they are 7 (8) and 15, which would give partially reproduced. With the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise the counts are 5 (6) and 18, and with spikethresh keeping the slow events 6 (7) and 20; each would give partially reproduced. In 2-mV bins the 33 values give 7, 8, 10, 4, 2 and 2 neurons, against 7, 8, 11, 3, 2 and 2 read from Figure 3B.

Result: reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption and on detail 1). Over the 29 neurons with the LFP flag, is 4.80 +- 0.52 mV before LFP-based culling and 3.19 +- 0.43 mV after it (paper 4.8 +- 0.5 and 3.1 +- 0.1; both within tolerance, the second by 0.01 mV), a fall of 33%. The peak-to-trough height over the trace (2b, 3.12 mV), the criteria after culling (5b, 3.04 mV) and heights re-measured after culling (3.07 mV) keep both values within tolerance. The peak searched in the culling window (1b) gives 2.99 mV after culling, and the variance over N 2.94 mV, both outside, which would not give reproduced. With the claims file's spike rule the values are 5.41 and 3.75 mV, both outside; with the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise 4.63 and 3.13 mV, both within; with spikethresh keeping the slow events 5.22 and 3.41 mV, the second outside.

fig5b-residual-lfp-psp-correlation¶

After LFP-based culling, PSP height still correlates with LFP height across trials for many tones, as in the 60 unculled responses to one tone of the Figure 5 neuron.

In [13]:
def residual_correlations(label):
    out = []
    for name in lfp_neurons:
        for r in PT[label][name]:
            if not ac2.included(r, "lfp"):
                continue
            k = r["keep_lfp"]
            h, s, lh = r["h"][k], r["s"][k], r["lfp_h"][k]
            rs, ps = stats.pearsonr(s, h)
            rl, pl = stats.pearsonr(lh, h)
            out.append({"neuron": name, "tone": r["tone"], "n": int(k.sum()), "r_scale": rs, "p_scale": ps,
                        "r_lfp_height": rl, "p_lfp_height": pl})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

for label in ("main", SPK, SPK_ANY, SPK_SLOW, "peak in culling window (1b)", "heights re-measured after culling"):
    rc = residual_correlations(label)
    print(f"[{label}] {len(rc)} tones of {rc.neuron.nunique()} neurons")
    for col in ("scale", "lfp_height"):
        r_, p_ = rc[f"r_{col}"], rc[f"p_{col}"]
        print(f"   LFP {col:10s}: positive {100 * (r_ > 0).mean():.0f}%, p < 0.05 {100 * (p_ < 0.05).mean():.0f}%"
              f" (positive and p < 0.05 {100 * ((r_ > 0) & (p_ < 0.05)).mean():.0f}%), median r {r_.median():.3f};"
              f" chance for p < 0.05 is 5%")

Result: reproduced. Over 396 included tones of the 29 neurons, after LFP-based culling, PSP height correlates positively with the LFP scale factor in 81% of tones and with p < 0.05 in 32% (30% positive and significant; 5% expected by chance), above the criterion's half and quarter. With the LFP peak height in place of the scale factor, 75% and 26%. The Figure 5 neuron (020701md01b, 63 repetitions) has two tones with 60 trials left after culling (31,118 and 5,527 Hz), with r = 0.70 and 0.65 to the scale factor (p < 0.001). With the claims file's spike rule, 405 tones, 79% positive and 31% with p < 0.05; with the two further spike rules 401 tones, 80% and 31%, and 79% and 32%; with heights re-measured after culling the same as the main reading.

fig7a-lfp-culling-estimation¶

LFP-based culling and estimation together reduce the variability index by 40% on average, to 2.9 mV across 29 neurons, reduce it in 26 of 29 neurons, by as much as 71%, and have little effect when total variability is already small.

Result: partially reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption and on detail 5). <q LFP-culled&estimation> is 2.69 +- 0.33 mV over 29 neurons (2.9 +- 0.3), and the procedures reduce tones in 26 of 29 neurons, as in the paper. The average reduction is 43.9% by reading (a) and 40.1% by reading (b), so the 40% holds. The largest reduction is 80.0% (030301md03b), outside 71 +- 7.1%. In that neuron LFP-based culling leaves 12 of its 18 included tones; four of the six it drops have q of 5.7 to 35.8 mV, so tones is 5.40 mV over all included tones and 1.73 mV over the 12 kept, before estimation brings it to 1.08 mV. In the four neurons with total tones below 1.5 mV the procedures lower it by 8.6 to 49.1%; shown, not scored. With the tone criteria applied after culling (5b) the value is 2.59 mV, 26 neurons are reduced and the largest reduction is 73.9%, which would give reproduced; with the claims file's spike rule the value is 3.22 mV, outside, which would give not reproduced. With the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise (2.68 mV, 27 reduced, largest 80.0%), with spikethresh keeping the slow events (2.85 mV, 29 reduced, 80.0%) and with heights re-measured after culling (2.62 mV, 26, 80.5%) the outcome is partially reproduced.

fig4c-psp-culling-can-increase¶

PSP-based culling reduces the tone-averaged variability for all but one neuron, but increases the variability for at least one tone in half (18/33) of the neurons; in the Figure 4 neuron, it raises q for a 9.2-kHz tone from 0.47 to 0.57 mV.

In [16]:
rows = []
for label, df in S.items():
    pt = PT[label] if label in PT else PT["main"]
    crit = SUMMARY_READINGS.get(label, {}).get("criteria", "before")
    up = 0
    for name, tones in pt.items():
        if any(ac2.included(r, None, crit) and ac2.included(r, "psp", crit) and r["q_psp"] > r["q"] for r in tones):
            up += 1
    d = df.dropna(subset=["q_psp"])
    rows.append({"reading": label, "<q> falls": int((d.q_psp < d.q).sum()), "of": len(d),
                 "neurons with a tone whose q rises": up})

Result: partially reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption and on measuring heights once before culling). PSP-based culling lowers tones in 32 of 33 neurons (the exception is 021401md02, whose one remaining tone rises from 5.19 to 10.98 mV), as the paper says. q rises for at least one tone in 16 of 33 neurons, outside 18 +- 1.8. Readings 1b, 2b, 3 and the intersected cullings give 16, as does spikethresh keeping the slow events; the claims file's spike rule and the criteria after culling (5b) 15, and without the negative scale factor rule in PSP culling (4b) 20, all outside. With heights re-measured after culling the count is 18, and with the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise 17; both are within tolerance, with 32 of 33 neurons falling, and would give reproduced.

The Figure 4 neuron. The search the claims file sets finds 11 tones in 8 neurons that fit the Figure 4B legend, and in none of them does the 9,188-Hz tone give 0.47 and 0.57 mV; the closest 9,188-Hz pair in any neuron is 0.470 to 0.502 mV, in 030301md03b. The panels of Figure 4 are labelled 030301md03b, so the paper names this neuron (asked of a reader, as the claims file reads it as not named). Its 9,188-Hz tone gives 0.470 mV before PSP-based culling, matching 0.47, and 0.502 mV after it, below 0.57 +- 0.057; the culled trial is the one aberrant trace that peaks about 10 ms after onset, as in Figure 4C. At 31,118 Hz (Figure 4A and 4B) PSP-based culling removes two of 16 trials: the trace that falls far below baseline, the paper's aberrant trial, and one with a negative scale factor. LFP-based culling removes four, including both. Without the negative scale factor rule in PSP culling (4b) it removes only the aberrant trace, and LFP-based culling removes that trace and three others, which is what the Figure 4B legend says. That fits reading 4b, while the Methods cite trials 3 and 8 of Figure 5C, a PSP-based culling panel, as trials with negative scale factors, which fits reading 4a. Reading 4a is kept.

fig7b-private-best-estimate¶

PSP-based culling followed by LFP-based culling and estimation reduces variability by as much as 85%, to a best estimate of private variability of 1.6 mV across 28 neurons, comparable and low for all neurons.

Result: reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption). The best estimate of private variability, PSP-based culling followed by LFP-based culling on the trials it keeps and estimation, is 1.48 +- 0.17 mV over 28 neurons (1.6 +- 0.2; 28 exact), and the largest reduction from total variability is 84.6% (85 +- 8.5). Deciding both cullings on the full ensemble gives 1.51 mV and 87.8%. The readings of details 1, 2, 4 and 5 give 1.42 to 1.78 mV and heights re-measured after culling 1.51 mV, all within tolerance; the variance over N, the claims file's variant of detail 3, gives 1.36 mV, just outside. With the claims file's spike rule the value is 2.01 mV, outside; with the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise 1.56 mV and with spikethresh keeping the slow events 1.72 mV, both within. The values are low for most neurons (0.31 to 2.80 mV) except 110900md05 (4.52 mV, three tones); their SD across neurons is 0.88 mV against 2.85 mV for total variability.

culling-controls¶

Random culling of as many traces as LFP-based culling removes leaves the variability index unchanged (4.5 against 4.6 mV), while matching the PSP-based or both cullings lowers it (3.67 and 2.98 mV) because tones with fewer than 10 non-aberrant trials drop out; keeping only those tones without culling gives 2.9 mV. PSP-based culling removes 29% of trials and LFP-based culling 38%.

In [18]:
def removed_mask(r, kind):
    if kind == "psp":
        return ~r["keep_psp"]
    if "keep_lfp" not in r:
        return None
    return ~r["keep_lfp"] if kind == "lfp" else ~r["keep_both"]

def random_control(pt, kind, names, seed, min_mean=ac2.MIN_MEAN, n_sims=20, ddof=1, min_left=ac2.MIN_TRIALS):
    """Remove at random, per neuron and tone, as many trials as the named culling removed, from the
    tones included before culling; keep the tones with at least `min_left` trials left (10: the tone
    criteria applied again; 2: not applied again) and take <q>neurons."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    sims, dropped = [], []
    for _ in range(n_sims):
        per_neuron, n_drop = [], 0
        for name in names:
            qs = []
            for r in pt[name]:
                if not ac2.included(r, None, min_mean=min_mean):
                    continue
                rem = removed_mask(r, kind)
                k = int(rem.sum()) if rem is not None else 0
                keep = rng.permutation(r["n"])[k:]
                if len(keep) >= max(min_left, 2):
                    qs.append(ac2.q_index(r["h"][keep], ddof))
                else:
                    n_drop += 1
            if qs:
                per_neuron.append(np.mean(qs))
        sims.append((np.mean(per_neuron), len(per_neuron)))
        dropped.append(n_drop)
    v = np.array([s[0] for s in sims])
    return {"mean": v.mean(), "SD over sims": v.std(ddof=1), "SE over sims": v.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n_sims),
            "neurons": int(np.median([s[1] for s in sims])), "tones dropped": float(np.mean(dropped))}

all_names, lfp_names = list(N), list(lfp_neurons)
def controls(label, min_mean=ac2.MIN_MEAN, min_left=ac2.MIN_TRIALS):
    pt = PT[label]
    out = {
        "LFP-matched, 29 neurons": random_control(pt, "lfp", lfp_names, 11, min_mean, min_left=min_left),
        "LFP-matched, 33 (4 unculled)": random_control(pt, "lfp", all_names, 12, min_mean, min_left=min_left),
        "PSP-matched, 33 neurons": random_control(pt, "psp", all_names, 13, min_mean, min_left=min_left),
        "PSP-matched, 29 neurons": random_control(pt, "psp", lfp_names, 14, min_mean, min_left=min_left),
        "both-matched, 29 neurons": random_control(pt, "both", lfp_names, 15, min_mean, min_left=min_left),
    }
    return pd.DataFrame(out).T

# Tones per neuron that the LFP-matched random control drops (fewer than 10 left), which are the
# tones that LFP-based culling itself drops, as it removes the same number; <q>tones over the rest.
drop = []
for name in lfp_names:
    inc = [r for r in PT["main"][name] if ac2.included(r)]
    left = [r for r in inc if r["n"] - int((~r["keep_lfp"]).sum()) >= ac2.MIN_TRIALS]
    drop.append({"neuron": name, "included": len(inc), "dropped": len(inc) - len(left),
                 "<q> all included": np.mean([r["q"] for r in inc]),
                 "<q> tones left": np.mean([r["q"] for r in left]) if left else np.nan})
drop = pd.DataFrame(drop).set_index("neuron")
print("\nLFP-matched control, tones dropped per neuron (main):")
print(drop.round(2).T.to_string())
print(f"Neurons losing every tone: {int((drop.dropped == drop.included).sum())}; mean of <q> over the tones left {drop['<q> tones left'].mean():.2f}"
      f" (n = {drop['<q> tones left'].notna().sum()}) against {drop['<q> all included'].mean():.2f} over all included tones")

def fraction_removed(pt, kind, names):
    pooled_rem = pooled_all = 0
    per = []
    for name in names:
        rem_n = all_n = 0
        for r in pt[name]:
            if not ac2.included(r):
                continue
            rem = removed_mask(r, kind)
            rem_n += int(rem.sum())
            all_n += r["n"]
        pooled_rem += rem_n
        pooled_all += all_n
        if all_n:
            per.append(rem_n / all_n)
    return 100 * pooled_rem / pooled_all, 100 * np.mean(per)

for label in ("main", SPK, SPK_ANY, SPK_SLOW, "peak-to-trough over trace (2b)", "no negative-f rule in PSP culling (4b)"):
    pt = PT[label]
    f_psp33 = fraction_removed(pt, "psp", all_names)
    f_psp29 = fraction_removed(pt, "psp", lfp_names)
    f_lfp = fraction_removed(pt, "lfp", lfp_names)
    f_both = fraction_removed(pt, "both", lfp_names)
    print(f"[{label}] trials removed, pooled / mean of neurons: PSP-based {f_psp33[0]:.1f}% / {f_psp33[1]:.1f}% (33 neurons),"
          f" {f_psp29[0]:.1f}% / {f_psp29[1]:.1f}% (29); LFP-based {f_lfp[0]:.1f}% / {f_lfp[1]:.1f}% (29); both {f_both[0]:.1f}% / {f_both[1]:.1f}%")

Result: not reproduced. Two of the four q values and one of the two fractions match. Random culling matched to both cullings gives 2.997 mV (2.98 +- 0.02) and the second control 2.96 +- 0.32 mV over 28 neurons (2.9 +- 0.3). Random culling matched to LFP-based culling gives 3.82 mV over the 29 LFP neurons (3.80 over 33), not the 4.5 +- 0.1 mV of the paper. It removes as many trials per tone as LFP-based culling, so it drops the same tones: 247 of the 643 included tones of the 29 neurons fall below 10 trials, and tones over the tones left averages 3.72 mV against 4.80 over all included tones. Without the tone criteria applied again after random culling, a reading that may be the paper's (asked of a reader), the LFP-matched control gives 4.83 mV (SD over simulations 0.97), within reach of 4.5, while the PSP-matched one becomes unstable (2.30 mV, SD 8.5, from tones left with few trials). Matched to PSP-based culling, with the criteria applied again, it gives 3.737 mV over 33 neurons (3.67 +- 0.02; the miss, 0.067, is more than three SEs) and 3.86 over 29. PSP-based culling removes 24.1% of the trials of included tones (pooled; 19.2% as a mean of neurons), outside 29 +- 2.9%, and LFP-based culling 37.8% (38 +- 3.8). With the claims file's spike rule the controls give 4.36, 3.74 and 3.98 mV, the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise 3.68, 3.92 and 3.10 mV, and spikethresh keeping the slow events 4.11, 5.09 and 3.47 mV; the outcome is the same. The controls use the heights measured on the full ensemble under every reading.

fig7d-large-responses¶

For tones with mean PSPs of at least 15 mV, total variability is lower (2.9 mV, 19 neurons) than for all tones, but the private variability is the same as for all tones (best estimate 1.5 mV, LFP-based bound 1.9 mV, 16 neurons).

Result: reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption and on details 1, 3 and 4). For tones with a mean PSP of at least 15 mV, total is 2.92 +- 0.36 mV over 19 neurons (2.9 +- 0.4; 19 exact), the LFP-based bound 1.62 +- 0.23 mV (1.9 +- 0.3) and the best estimate 1.43 +- 0.20 mV (1.5 +- 0.2). The LFP-based bound is within tolerance by 0.02 mV. The peak searched in the culling window (1b) gives 1.57 mV and the variance over N 1.50 mV, both below 1.6, which would not give reproduced; without the negative scale factor rule in PSP culling (4b) it is 1.61 mV, within by 0.01, and with heights re-measured after culling 1.65 mV. Both private values come from 14 neurons, not the paper's 16; with the 3 mV and 15 mV criteria applied after culling (detail 5b) there are 15 and 16, with values 1.81 and 1.52 mV, also within. With the claims file's spike rule total is 6.13 mV over 21 neurons, which would give not reproduced, as would spikethresh keeping the slow events (5.50 mV over 21). With the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise the values are 3.00, 1.99 and 1.71 mV, the last 0.01 mV outside.

large-responses-controls¶

For tones of at least 15 mV, random culling and keeping only tones that survive both cullings give 3.2 mV, so the private estimate of 1.5 mV is not an undersampling effect.

cv-large-responses¶

In coefficient of variation, both the total and the private variability of the large (at least 15 mV) responses are lower than for the full data set (total 0.37 against 0.73; private 0.27 against 0.41, significantly lower), unlike the variability index.

Result: partially reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption and on details 2, 4 and 5). Total CV is 0.371 +- 0.027 for tones of at least 15 mV (19 neurons) and 0.734 +- 0.042 for all tones (33), matching 0.37 and 0.73. Private CV is 0.265 +- 0.021 (14 neurons) against 0.383 +- 0.026 (28): the first is within 0.27 +- 0.01 and the second 0.007 below 0.41 +- 0.02. The private CV of large responses is significantly lower under both readings of the test (Student's t, p = 0.0055; paired over 14 neurons, p < 0.0001). The criterion's reproduced outcome needs all four values, so the claim holds in part. With the peak-to-trough height over the whole trace (2b) the private values are 0.268 and 0.402 and all four hold; with the negative scale factor rule left out of PSP culling (4b) 0.282 and 0.424, and with the criteria after culling (5b) 0.278 and 0.380, one out each time. With the claims file's spike rule the large-response total CV is 0.491 and the private difference is not significant (p = 0.475 and 0.380); spikethresh keeping the slow events gives 0.468 and p = 0.136 and 0.081. With the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise the private values are 0.286 and 0.389 and the difference is significant (p = 0.014), and with heights re-measured after culling 0.267 and 0.385; one or two values out, partially reproduced.

lfp-cv-not-different¶

The LFP recorded with the more variable neurons is not more variable than that recorded with the less variable neurons (CV 0.66 against 0.74, P = 0.5), so differences in total variability are not explained by gross state differences seen in the LFP.

In [22]:
def lfp_cv(label, measure):
    out = {}
    for name in lfp_neurons:
        vals = []
        for r in PT[label][name]:
            if not ac2.included(r):
                continue
            x = r["lfp_h"] if measure == "height" else r["s"]
            vals.append(np.std(x, ddof=1) / np.mean(x))
        out[name] = np.mean(vals)
    return pd.Series(out)

for label in ("main", SPK, SPK_ANY, SPK_SLOW):
    q29 = S[label].q[lfp_neurons].sort_values(ascending=False)
    more, less = q29.index[:14], q29.index[14:]
    for measure in ("height", "scale factor"):
        cv = lfp_cv(label, measure)
        t, p = stats.ttest_ind(cv[more], cv[less])
        print(f"[{label}; LFP {measure}] more variable (14): {mse(cv[more])}; less variable (15): {mse(cv[less])};"
              f" Student's t = {t:.2f}, p = {p:.3f}; difference {cv[more].mean() - cv[less].mean():.3f}")
cvh = lfp_cv("main", "height")
print("\nLFP CV per neuron (height, main):", cvh.round(2).to_dict())
print("Mean LFP height sign check: tones whose mean LFP height is negative:",
      sum(np.mean(r["lfp_h"]) < 0 for name in lfp_neurons for r in PT["main"][name] if ac2.included(r)))

Result: reproduced. Ranking the 29 LFP neurons by total tones, the LFP height CV is 0.61 +- 0.05 for the 14 more variable and 0.57 +- 0.06 for the 15 less variable neurons (paper 0.66 +- 0.06 and 0.74 +- 0.09); Student's t-test finds no difference (t = 0.43, p = 0.674; difference 0.035). The less variable group's CV is below the paper's tolerance. The LFP scale factor CV gives 0.89 against 0.77 (p = 0.350), and the claims file's spike rule p = 0.428 (0.55 against 0.62). Unlike the paper's slight opposite trend, the more variable neurons have the slightly higher LFP CV here. With the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise the LFP height CVs are 0.65 and 0.53 (p = 0.118), and with spikethresh keeping the slow events 0.56 and 0.61 (p = 0.511); neither finds a difference.

anesthesia-comparison¶

Total variability does not differ significantly between the three anesthesia protocols (pentobarbital 3.7, pentobarbital with diazepam 6.1, urethane 5.0 mV), and private variability differs slightly but significantly between pentobarbital alone (1.1 mV) and urethane (2.2 mV).

    for an in ("P", "P_with_Diaz", "U"):

    row["private P vs U t p"] = stats.ttest_ind(pp, pu).pvalue
    row["private P vs U Mann-Whitney p"] = stats.mannwhitneyu(pp, pu).pvalue
    rows.append(row)

Result: reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption and on details 1, 3, 4 and 5). Total is 3.69 +- 0.70 (pentobarbital, 13), 6.15 +- 2.81 (with diazepam, 3) and 4.99 +- 0.58 mV (urethane, 17), all within tolerance; neither the one-way ANOVA (p = 0.251) nor Kruskal-Wallis (p = 0.354) finds a difference. The private best estimate is 1.01 +- 0.13 (12), 1.37 +- 0.33 (3) and 1.93 +- 0.29 mV (13), with the paper's group sizes (12, 3, 13), all within tolerance, two of them by 0.01 and 0.03 mV; pentobarbital alone and urethane differ (Student's t p = 0.0094; Mann-Whitney p = 0.0083). The margins are small and the readings move them across: deciding both cullings on the full ensemble gives 0.98 mV for pentobarbital, the peak in the culling window (1b) 1.82 and the criteria after culling (5b) 1.84 mV for urethane, and leaving the negative scale factor rule out of PSP culling (4b) 2.51 mV for urethane, and the variance over N 0.93 mV for pentobarbital, each of which would give partially reproduced. With the peak-to-trough height over the trace (2b) and with heights re-measured after culling (1.01, 1.34 and 2.01 mV; t p = 0.0063) every value holds. With the claims file's spike rule the urethane total is 6.42 mV and the ANOVA finds a difference (p = 0.039), which would give not reproduced. With the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise every value holds and the tests agree (ANOVA p = 0.199, private t p = 0.0064); with spikethresh keeping the slow events the urethane total is 6.00 mV, outside, which would not give reproduced.

fig8-spontaneous-veto¶

The size of spontaneous activity before the stimulus is anticorrelated with the evoked PSP, in the LFP (mean correlation -0.14, 29 neurons) and in the whole-cell record (-0.22, 33 neurons), the whole-cell correlation being negative in 30 of 33 neurons.

The 100 ms before each tone come from the sweeps (pre_wc, pre_lfp). For the first tone of a sweep this window overlaps the prepulse in neurons whose prepulse ends after 100 ms; those trials are left out (counted below).

In [24]:
def spont_size(x, channel, reading):
    if reading == "a":
        return x.max(1) - x.min(1)
    dev = x - x.mean(1, keepdims=True)
    return dev.max(1) if channel == "wc" else np.abs(dev).max(1)

def veto(label, channel, size_reading, corr_reading, window="100 ms", drop_spiking=False):
    """Correlation of the spontaneous event before each tone with the PSP height, per neuron.
    window "100 ms": the 100 ms before onset; "-100 to -15 ms": without the 15-ms baseline of the
    PSP height. drop_spiking: leave out trials with a spike in the window (the neuron's spikethresh
    above the trace's 15-ms baseline)."""
    out, dropped = {}, 0
    names = all_names if channel == "wc" else lfp_names
    stop = ac2.PRESTIM if window == "100 ms" else ac2.PRESTIM - ac2.PRE
    for name in names:
        n = N[name]
        pre = n["pre_wc"] if channel == "wc" else n["pre_lfp"]
        per_tone, pooled_x, pooled_h = [], [], []
        for r in PT[label][name]:
            if not ac2.included(r):
                continue
            ok = ~n["prestim_overlaps_prepulse"][r["trials"]]
            if drop_spiking:
                wc = n["pre_wc"][r["trials"], :stop] - n["rbaseline"][r["trials"], None]
                ok &= wc.max(1) <= n["params"]["spikethresh"]
            dropped += int((~ok).sum())
            x = spont_size(pre[r["trials"], :stop].astype(float), channel, size_reading)[ok]
            h = r["h"][ok]
            if len(h) >= 3 and np.ptp(x) > 0:
                per_tone.append(stats.pearsonr(x, h)[0])
                pooled_x.append(x)
                pooled_h.append(h / h.mean())
        if per_tone:
            out[name] = np.mean(per_tone) if corr_reading == "a" else stats.pearsonr(
                np.concatenate(pooled_x), np.concatenate(pooled_h))[0]
    return pd.Series(out), dropped

def veto_rows(labels, windows, spiking):
    rows = []
    for label in labels:
        for window in windows:
            for ds in spiking:
                for sr in ("a", "b"):
                    for cr in ("a", "b"):
                        wc, dropped = veto(label, "wc", sr, cr, window, ds)
                        lf, _ = veto(label, "lfp", sr, cr, window, ds)
                        rows.append({"reading": label, "window": window, "spiking trials out": ds, "size": sr, "correlation": cr,
                                     "LFP mean r": lf.mean(), "LFP SE": lf.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(lf)), "LFP n": len(lf),
                                     "LFP negative": int((lf < 0).sum()),
                                     "WC mean r": wc.mean(), "WC SE": wc.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(wc)), "WC n": len(wc),
                                     "WC negative": int((wc < 0).sum()), "trials left out": dropped})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

Result: reproduced. Under readings (a) size as maximum minus minimum and (b) one correlation over all trials with heights normalized by the tone's mean, the mean correlation is -0.155 +- 0.028 for the LFP (29 neurons; -0.14 +- 0.02) and -0.193 +- 0.031 for the whole cell (33; -0.22 +- 0.03), negative in 29 of 33 neurons (30 +- 3). Under readings (b, b) -0.149, -0.210 and 28 also hold. Under (a, a) the LFP mean, -0.168, is outside its tolerance. All combinations, with either spike rule, give negative means for both channels (-0.143 to -0.168 LFP, -0.179 to -0.238 whole cell). The 15-ms baseline of the PSP height lies inside the 100-ms window, so a depolarization just before onset lowers the height by construction. With the window ending 15 ms before onset, so that it does not overlap the baseline, the correlations remain (-0.134 to -0.158 LFP, -0.172 to -0.220 whole cell), and under (a, a) and (b, b) all three values hold (-0.158, -0.220, 29; -0.135, -0.202, 28); under (a, b) the whole-cell mean, -0.172, is outside. With the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise, (b, b) gives -0.155, -0.205 and 29, and with spikethresh keeping the slow events -0.146, -0.201 and 28, all within; under (a, b) the whole-cell means (-0.187, -0.181) are outside. Leaving out trials with a spike in the window changes the means by at most 0.014. 257 trials whose window overlaps the prepulse are left out.

overfitting-correction-example¶

For the Figure 5 neuron, the shuffle control attributes 0.02 mV to overfitting of the linear estimator, and the corrected value after both cullings and estimation is 0.57 mV.

Correction per tone (detail 7) gives the same tone average as per neuron: mean(est + q - shuf) = mean(est) + mean(q) - mean(shuf).
Trials left per tone after both cullings: [52, 57, 58, 46, 59, 51, 53, 59, 51, 57, 57, 58, 54, 55, 59, 59, 54]

Result: reproduced (resting on details 2 and 4). In the Figure 5 neuron (020701md01b), after both cullings tones is 0.757 mV (0.76), the shuffled estimation gives 0.743 mV (0.74), the estimation 0.524 mV uncorrected (0.55) and 0.537 mV corrected (0.57); all four within 10%. The overfitting share is 0.014 mV against the paper's 0.02. The values are the same with the claims file's spike rule (no spike trials in this neuron) and nearly so with the cullings decided on the full ensemble (0.759, 0.746, 0.525, 0.538). With the peak-to-trough height over the whole trace (2b) they are 1.118, 1.085, 0.859 and 0.892 mV, and without the negative scale factor rule in PSP culling (4b) 0.986, 0.971, 0.627 and 0.643 mV; in both the corrected value is outside, which would give not reproduced. Per-tone and per-neuron corrections give the same tone average (the identity printed above), so detail 7's per-tone reading needs no run of its own. The two further spike rules and the peak in the culling window give the main values, the variance over N 0.743, 0.730, 0.514 and 0.528 mV and heights re-measured after culling 0.756, 0.742, 0.522 and 0.536 mV, all within.

private-shared-ranges¶

The private component of the variability is small, about 1 to 3 mV, and relatively homogeneous across neurons, while the shared component is often much larger and more heterogeneous, ranging from about 0 to 10 mV.

Result: partially reproduced. Two of the three parts hold. Shared variability (total minus private) ranges from 0.25 to 9.26 mV with total over all included tones, and 0.10 to 5.31 mV with total over the tones kept for the private estimate, both within -1 to 11 mV, and its SD across neurons (2.60 or 1.38 mV) exceeds that of private variability (0.88 mV). But only 20 of 28 neurons (71%) have a private value between 0.9 and 3.3 mV, short of the 80% the criterion sets: seven are below 0.9 mV (0.31 to 0.83) and one is above (4.52 mV). Every reading gives 57% to 75%, so the outcome is the same under all of them.

quantal-comparison¶

In 14 of 33 neurons at least one tone elicits responses whose variability index is within a factor of 2 of the 0.38 mV expected from stochastic release alone.

Result: reproduced. 14 of 33 neurons have at least one included tone with q within a factor of 2 of 0.38 mV, under both readings of "within a factor of 2" (the smallest q is 0.14 mV, but that neuron has another tone within range). With 0.39 mV the count is 15, also within 14 +- 1.4. The claims file's spike rule, the two further spike rules and the peak in the culling window give the same counts; with the variance over N, the claims file's variant of detail 3, 17 and 20.

mepsp-size¶

Miniature EPSPs recorded in vivo after TTX have a mean size of 0.39 mV with a CV of 0.36 across 6 neurons, consistent with in vitro estimates.

The paper gives no detection method. Two standard detectors are run (claims file readings a and b): (a) template matching (Clements and Bekkers 1997; template rise 0.5 ms, decay 5 ms), with a threshold on the ratio of the fitted scale to its standard error and the fitted scale as the size; (b) a threshold on the derivative of the trace smoothed over 1 ms, in noise SDs of that derivative, with the size taken as the peak in the 10 ms after onset minus the mean of the 2 ms before it. The traces are digitized in steps of 0.049 mV, so most differences between samples are 0; the noise SD is the SD after clipping at 3 SD, which does not collapse (the median-based SD is printed beside it). Each detector is also run on the sign-inverted trace: mEPSPs are depolarizing, so the events found there estimate the false positives at that threshold. Sweeps are those of each recording's stable epoch (first_trial to last_trial), without their first 0.3 s (prepulse); which file is trial k is not documented, so three mappings are run. One recording, 030401md02h, is divided by its documented gain of 4.

In [28]:

# Each detector and threshold, on the trace and on the inverted trace, per recording and mapping.
KS = (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8)
def detect(x, fs, det, k):
    return ac2.minis_template(x, fs, k) if det == "template" else ac2.minis_derivative(x, fs, k)

rows, EVENTS = [], {}
for order in ("numeric", "dir", "all"):
    for name, rec in D["ttx"].items():
        fs = 1.0 / rec["dx"]
        sweeps = ac2.mini_sweeps(rec, order)
        secs = sum(len(s) for s in sweeps.values()) / fs
        for det in ("template", "derivative"):
            for k in KS:
                pos = {i: detect(s, fs, det, k) for i, s in sweeps.items()}
                n_neg = sum(len(detect(-s, fs, det, k)["onsets"]) for s in sweeps.values())
                size = np.concatenate([e["scale" if det == "template" else "size"] for e in pos.values()])
                t_on = np.concatenate([e["onsets"] / fs + ac2.MINI_SKIP_S for e in pos.values()])
                EVENTS[order, name, det, k] = pos
                rows.append({"mapping": order, "recording": name, "detector": det, "k": k, "seconds": secs,
                             "events": len(size), "rate_hz": len(size) / secs, "inverted_rate_hz": n_neg / secs,
                             "inverted/trace": n_neg / len(size) if len(size) else np.nan,
                             "mean_mV": size.mean() if len(size) else np.nan,
                             "cv": size.std(ddof=1) / size.mean() if len(size) > 1 else np.nan,
                             "in 50 ms after a tone": np.mean((t_on - 0.2) % 0.5 < 0.05) if len(size) else np.nan})
minis = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("Numeric mapping, per recording:")
print(minis[minis.mapping == "numeric"].drop(columns="mapping").round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("\nMean over recordings (paper: 0.39 +- 0.08 mV, CV 0.36 +- 0.03, n = 6); 'in 50 ms after a tone' is 0.10 by chance:")
summ = minis.groupby(["mapping", "detector", "k"]).agg(
    mean_size=("mean_mV", "mean"), se_size=("mean_mV", lambda x: x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(x.notna().sum())),
    mean_cv=("cv", "mean"), recordings=("mean_mV", "count"), rate_hz=("rate_hz", "mean"),
    inverted_over_trace=("inverted/trace", "mean"), after_tone=("in 50 ms after a tone", "mean"))
print(summ.round(3).to_string())

# Main reading: the derivative detector at, for each recording, the lowest k at which the inverted
# trace gives at most 10% as many events as the trace (a false-positive bound chosen here); 5% and
# 20% are shown. A recording with no such k has no events counted.
def by_fp(order, bound, det="derivative"):
    m = minis[(minis.mapping == order) & (minis.detector == det) & (minis.events > 1)]
    ok = m[m["inverted/trace"] <= bound].sort_values("k").groupby("recording").head(1).set_index("recording")
    return ok[["k", "events", "rate_hz", "inverted/trace", "mean_mV", "cv"]]

for order in ("numeric", "dir", "all"):
    for bound in (0.05, 0.10, 0.20):
        for det in ("derivative", "template"):
            t = by_fp(order, bound, det)
            print(f"[{order}; {det}; inverted/trace <= {bound:.2f}] {len(t)} recordings: mean size {t.mean_mV.mean():.3f}"
                  f" +- {t.mean_mV.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(t)):.3f} mV, mean CV {t.cv.mean():.3f}" if len(t) > 1 else
                  f"[{order}; {det}; inverted/trace <= {bound:.2f}] {len(t)} recordings")
MAIN_MINI = by_fp("numeric", 0.10)
print("\nMain reading per recording:")
print(MAIN_MINI.round(3).to_string())
rest = MAIN_MINI.drop(index="030401md02h")
print(f"Main reading without 030401md02h (offset and gain questioned): {len(rest)} recordings, mean size"
      f" {rest.mean_mV.mean():.3f} +- {rest.mean_mV.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(rest)):.3f} mV, mean CV {rest.cv.mean():.3f}")

# Event-triggered averages and size histograms under the main reading.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(18, 5.5))
ranges = []
for j, name in enumerate(D["ttx"]):
    rec = D["ttx"][name]
    fs = 1.0 / rec["dx"]
    ax[0, j].set_title(name, fontsize=9)
    if name not in MAIN_MINI.index:
        ax[0, j].text(0.5, 0.5, "no k passes", ha="center", transform=ax[0, j].transAxes)
        continue
    k = int(MAIN_MINI.loc[name, "k"])
    sweeps = ac2.mini_sweeps(rec, "numeric")
    seg = []
    for i, e in EVENTS["numeric", name, "derivative", k].items():
        x = ac2._smooth(sweeps[i], fs)
        for o in e["onsets"]:
            if o >= 40 and o + 120 < len(x):
                seg.append(x[o - 40:o + 120] - x[o - 8:o].mean())
    seg = np.array(seg)
    t = (np.arange(-40, 120)) / fs * 1000
    ax[0, j].plot(t, seg.mean(0), "k")
    ax[0, j].fill_between(t, np.percentile(seg, 25, 0), np.percentile(seg, 75, 0), color="0.8")
    ax[0, j].set(xlabel="ms from onset", ylabel="mV")
    sizes = np.concatenate([e["size"] for e in EVENTS["numeric", name, "derivative", k].values()])
    ax[1, j].hist(sizes, bins=20, color="0.4")
    ax[1, j].set(xlabel=f"size (mV), k = {k}", ylabel="events")
    ranges.append((name, len(seg), seg.mean(0).min(), seg.mean(0).max(), sizes.min(), sizes.max()))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
for name, n_ev, lo, hi, smin, smax in ranges:
    print(f"{name}: {n_ev} events averaged, average {lo:.2f} to {hi:.2f} mV; sizes {smin:.2f} to {smax:.2f} mV (all within the axes)")

Result: partially reproduced (resting on the assumed detector and threshold). The traces are
digitized in steps of 0.049 mV (0.012 mV for 030401md02h after its gain of 4), and 14% to 68% of
the differences between samples are 0. Template matching at thresholds of 3 to 5 finds up to 29
events per s, and on the inverted traces 55% to 80% as many (mean over the six recordings), so
most of those events are noise. Its mean size, 0.28 to 0.35 mV at
those thresholds, does not measure mEPSPs. The derivative detector finds fewer events on the
inverted traces. Its main reading takes, per recording, the lowest threshold at which the
inverted trace gives at most 10% as many events (k = 3 to 6). That gives a mean size of 0.602 +-
0.164 mV over five recordings, outside 0.39 +- 0.08, and a mean CV of 0.354, within 0.36 +- 0.03.
050401md02 has one stable sweep (7.7 s), and no threshold keeps its false positives below the
bound. The event-triggered averages of the main reading rise within about 2 ms and decay over
10 to 20 ms, peaking at 0.15 to 0.99 mV. The detected events are not locked to the tones played
during the recordings: 6.7% to 12.0% of them fall in the 50 ms after a tone, against 10% by chance.
The result depends on the detector, threshold and mapping of sweeps. With a fixed threshold, the
derivative detector gives 0.370 mV with CV 0.421 at k = 3 (mean holds) and 0.487 mV with CV 0.350
at k = 4 (CV holds). False-positive bounds of 5% and 20% give 0.702 and 0.549 mV (CV 0.314 and
0.376). The documentation's file order (dir) gives 0.726 mV and CV 0.296 under the main rule.
Under no reading with the false positives bounded do both values hold. The mean over recordings
rests on the threshold each recording gets: event rates under the main reading range from 0.11
Hz (030401md02h, 15 events, 1.04 mV) to 19 Hz (050801md01c, 0.20 mV, sizes down to 0.01 mV).
Without 030401md02h, whose offset and gain are questioned (data check), the four others give
0.492 mV and CV 0.385, both outside. The derivative detector
with a false-positive bound is adopted as an assumption, because it is the only one of the
claims file's two readings whose events are not mostly noise here.






















recording-properties¶


Each tone was presented 18 times on average (10 to 63) per neuron; rest potential ranged from
-58 to -92 mV (median -70) after junction potential correction, and input resistance from 19
to 141 MOhm (median 64).

Result: reproduced (resting on the assumption that input resistance excludes the access
resistance). Repetitions per tone: 18.12 +- 1.93 (SE), 10 to 63, as in the paper. Rest
potential from the 15-ms baselines, corrected by -12 mV: median -70.0 mV, range -58.4 to -92.0,
as in the paper; from the sweeps outside the prepulse, median -68.6 and range -55.3 to -87.9
(within the widened range). Input resistance from the prepulse is 58.2 to 438.3 MOhm (median
137.9) as measured; minus the recorded access resistance, which the uncompensated step includes,
it is 19.1 to 140.6 MOhm (median 65.1), as in the paper (19 to 141, median 64). The step response
alone does not match.






















access-resistance-depth-no-effect¶


Response variability is not correlated with access resistance (4.2 against 4.9 mV on either
side of the 60 MOhm median) and does not vary systematically with recording depth.




















In [32]:






ra = cells.R_access.astype(float)
depth = cells.depth_um.astype(float)
med = ra.median()
print(f"Access resistance: median {med:.1f} MOhm, range {ra.min():.0f} to {ra.max():.0f}; neurons at the median: {list(ra.index[ra == med])}")
print(f"Depth (Sutter travel / sqrt 2): {depth.notna().sum()} of 33 recorded, {depth.min():.0f} to {depth.max():.0f} um (paper: 180 to 834)")
for label in ("main", SPK, SPK_ANY, SPK_SLOW):
    q = S[label].q
    for placement, above in (("median cell with the upper group", ra >= med), ("median cell with the lower group", ra > med)):
        print(f"[{label}; {placement}] above median {mse(q[above])}; below {mse(q[~above])}")
    for var, x in (("access resistance", ra), ("depth", depth)):
        ok = x.notna()
        pr, pp = stats.pearsonr(x[ok], q[ok])
        sr, sp = stats.spearmanr(x[ok], q[ok])
        print(f"[{label}] {var}: Pearson r = {pr:.3f}, p = {pp:.3f}; Spearman rho = {sr:.3f}, p = {sp:.3f} (n = {ok.sum()})")

Result: reproduced (resting on the spike-rule assumption). The median access resistance is
60 MOhm (10 to 320).  is 4.88 +- 0.71 mV for the 17 neurons at or above the median and 4.27
+- 0.63 mV for the 16 below it, both within the tolerances of 4.2 +- 0.7 and 4.9 +- 0.7. The
values fit the paper's numbers better the other way round: here the higher access resistance
group is the more variable, where the paper has it the less variable. Neither Pearson (r =
0.087, p = 0.631) nor Spearman (rho = 0.155, p = 0.390) finds a correlation with access
resistance, nor with depth over the 25 neurons with a recorded depth (r = -0.273, p = 0.187; rho
= -0.338, p = 0.098). With the claims file's spike rule the groups are 5.70 and 4.99 mV, the
first outside its tolerance, and no correlation is significant (p = 0.125 to 0.661), which would
not give reproduced. With the corrected potential above -20 mV at any rise the groups are 4.50
and 4.36 mV, both within, and no correlation is significant; with spikethresh keeping the slow
events the upper group is 5.22 mV, outside.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the
reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.


How the analysis differs from the paper's. The paper links no code. Trials are each neuron's
stable epoch as given in the data set's cell_specific_parameters.m (its length matches the
paper's repetitions: mean 18.1, 10 to 63). Spike trials are found with the data set's
per-neuron threshold, an assumption. The claims file's rule (a fast rise, taken here as above 10
mV/ms, to above -20 mV after the junction potential correction) misses slow depolarizations to
about -10 mV, which may be regenerative events or large PSPs, broad spikes that cross -20 mV with
a rise below 10 mV/ms, and narrow spikes that peak below -20 mV; it raises  from 4.58 to 5.35
mV. Without the rise criterion the -20 mV rule gives 4.43 mV, and spikethresh keeping the slow
events 5.11 mV. All four rules are shown for every claim. The peak of the mean PSP is
searched over the whole trace after onset; the peak-to-trough height for culling is taken over the
culling window; negative scale factors are removed in both cullings; the tone criteria use the
mean before culling; heights are measured once before culling, and re-measuring them after
culling is shown as a reading (of the claims it is run for, it changes only fig4c, to
reproduced; the random culling controls keep the heights of the full ensemble). LFP-based culling follows
PSP-based culling and is run on the trials it keeps, as the Figure 6 legend says; deciding both
cullings on the full ensemble is shown as a reading. The overfitting correction averages 20
shuffles. Each open detail is run under the readings the claims file lists, and the tables above
show where they change an outcome. Input resistance is taken as the prepulse response minus the
recorded access resistance. mEPSPs are detected with a threshold on the derivative, set per
recording by a bound on the events found in the inverted trace; template matching and fixed
thresholds are shown. The panels drawn as Figures 2, 3A, 3B and 4 match the paper's by eye; the
paper labels its Figure 2 and 3A neuron 022801md01b, the one identified here, and its Figure 4
neuron 030301md03b.


What was found about the data set. It holds the 33 neurons, the 29 LFP flags, the anesthetic
groups and the six TTX recordings the paper describes, and with the per-neuron stable epochs and
spike thresholds of cell_specific_parameters.m the paper's population values follow closely
( 4.58, 4.80 with LFP, 2.19 after PSP-based culling, 3.19 after LFP-based culling, 1.48 for
the best private estimate). Those files are not described for these neurons. The documentation
gives a junction potential of about 10 mV and says the true potentials are about 10 mV more
depolarized than recorded; the paper subtracts 12 mV, and only that reproduces its rest
potentials. It calls the prepulse height a voltage in mV, while the values are currents in pA.
Depth is missing for 8 of 33 neurons. The TTX recording 030401md02h, after its documented
division by 4, sits near +2.6 mV, which is not a membrane potential. Which sweep file of a TTX
recording is trial k of its first_trial and last_trial is not documented, and the
documentation's own reading code lists the files in name order, which picks different sweeps
from the numeric order in four of the six recordings.
